First, notice that since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/964f8ac9ca9c305faef8562f66d063f318ecbe402df337377bd9efdf61301567.png) 
 we must have

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = e^y\cos x ,  
\qquad 
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} =e^y\sin x .
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(\pi,0).$ This gives

source.value:
For a function $f: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/7444a8128c085d7bf4f56a57a60c260864a50da0b744b6dbe22a2ced89a0588d.png)

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/22dd960829ea268e5aade685b56949f8998f87ae8c040a90f04436cbfc6b9a58.png)

In our case, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/4fede2bb5c2306f62b55b7996488baee52c69e7d41b011e0e9d2b7405e63a8f4.png)

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{y}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{y})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{y} & {x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y})=2\text{ }\,{e}^{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{y})=2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y})=2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{y})={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{ }\,{e}^{y} & 2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y} \\ 2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y} & {x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $\left(1,0\right).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,0)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
For a function $f: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/af5524049f5f8b3c4c4241520f2d874b454d61b1b025362f5193437f766e610b.png)

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/8882516e2732e419efdfb8439265212dd4f380d6a6ea58f6ff1291030bf50bfb.png)

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(\mathbf x) = \det \left( \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf x) \right)
$$

In our case, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/4fede2bb5c2306f62b55b7996488baee52c69e7d41b011e0e9d2b7405e63a8f4.png)

First, notice that since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/9252d1ce4f5df828f45351d01e0709cf2f2ca5df2c9c25390c111f40ca00fb22.png) we must have

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \ln y, 
\qquad 
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y})=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y})=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,1) = 0 \cdot 0 - 1\cdot 1 = -1.
$$
